common_name: Pentland Brig Kale (Scottish Dual-Purpose Leaf-and-Spring-Shoot Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring for a fall/winter crop, or sow in mid-summer for overwintering; Pentland Brig is exceptionally cold-hardy and is grown through winter specifically to produce tender flowering shoots the following spring.

directions: Sow directly or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow the tall, semi-open habit room to develop. Pentland Brig was bred in the 1960s at the Scottish Plant Breeding Station from a cross of Thousand-Head kale and curly kale, combining loose, lightly frilled, medium-green leaves with an unusual second act: overwintered plants send up abundant tender flowering shoots in early spring that are harvested and cooked exactly like sprouting broccoli. This dual-purpose habit, cut-and-come-again leaves through autumn and winter, then a flush of sweet flower shoots in the notorious late-winter hungry gap before other vegetables are ready, is what has kept it a favorite kitchen-garden variety in Britain for decades even though it remains uncommon in American seed catalogs. The flavor is notably mild and sweet for a kale, without the toughness of older curly types, and both the leaves and the immature flower buds are good raw or lightly cooked. Choose Pentland Brig where reliable winter survival and an early-spring harvest gap-filler matter more than a single big autumn leaf crop.

common_name: Beedy's Camden Kale (Maine Heirloom Overwintering Curly Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring, or sow in late summer for a fall crop and overwintering in mild climates; Beedy's Camden is unusually tender for such a cold-hardy kale and tends to self-sow readily where left to flower.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or space plants 12-18 inches apart and harvest outer leaves as needed. Beedy's Camden traces to a single kale plant that gardener Beedy Parker noticed overwintering in her Camden, Maine garden in the 1980s; she saved and shared its seed for years before Fedco Seeds arranged commercial production, introducing it more widely in 2009. The semi-savoyed, ruffled, medium-green leaves are notably more tender than the true Siberian types it resembles, staying pleasant through summer heat while also surviving hard New England winters, and the flavor turns markedly sweeter after several fall frosts. Its ready self-seeding habit and strong regional pedigree have made it a favorite among Northeast market growers and seed savers looking for a genuinely open-pollinated, locally adapted alternative to hybrid curly kales.

common_name: Trafalgar Brussels Sprout (Late Mid-Season F1 Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; Trafalgar is a late mid-season hybrid that fills the harvest window from mid-November into January, sweetening further with each hard frost.

directions: Start seeds indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil and stake the medium-tall stems against wind; top the plants once lower sprouts reach marble size to even out ripening, and harvest from the bottom up as sprouts firm up. Trafalgar is a British-bred F1 hybrid valued for producing abundant, uniformly round, tightly wrapped sprouts with a sweet, low-bitterness flavor that holds up well through a long late-season harvest window running from mid-autumn into the new year. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew and reliable, heavy-yielding habit have made it a standard late mid-season choice in UK trial and market gardens, and the sprouts stand well on the stalk without splitting, giving flexibility about exactly when to pick. Choose Trafalgar when the goal is a long stretch of classic, mild-flavored sprouts spanning Thanksgiving through the winter holidays rather than a single early flush.

common_name: Doric Brussels Sprout (RHS AGM Early Season F1 Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; Doric is a sturdy, shorter-statured early variety well suited to exposed or windy gardens, cropping from November into February.

directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant firmly into rich, well-drained soil and firm the base of each plant well since Doric's strength is its short, sturdy stem rather than height; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward as they firm and tighten. Doric is a widely grown F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, prized for its strong, compact, wind-resistant stems and heavy yields of smooth, bright, tightly rounded sprouts with good resistance to fusarium and useful tolerance of white blister and mildew. Because the plants stay shorter and stockier than many hybrids, staking needs are minimal even in exposed sites, and the whole stalk can be cut and stood in a cool spot to extend the usable harvest well past when the sprouts would otherwise be picked. Doric's long cropping window, from late autumn through midwinter, and its dependable disease tolerance make it a practical workhorse choice for a sustained home sprout harvest.
